sweep_summary: Dieri (dier1241) is coded fixed-dominant (initial primary; secondary on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable roots and on the first syllable of disyllabic suffixes; never final) on Austin 2021/1981 §2.5 p. 41, verified in the held grammar. Six stress-title items: all six are about Diyari word stress except Halle & Vergnaud 1987, whose Diyari content could not be verified (controlled-lending only). Two were downloaded open and read: Crowhurst 1994 (ROA-19 = WCCFL 13, 1995; OT analysis on Austin 1981 / Poser 1989 data) and Pensalfini 2000 (ALS99 proceedings, now served by als.asn.au; the Glottolog UWA URL is dead). Both restate Austin's pattern verbatim-consistently (initial stress in every morpheme of 2+ syllables, 3rd syllable of quadrisyllabic morphemes, monosyllabic suffixes never stressed, feet never cross a morpheme boundary) and confirm the classification; neither is first-hand and neither supersedes Austin. Poser 1989 (Phonology 6, DOI 10.1017/S0952675700000968) remains paywalled (Unpaywall/OpenAlex closed, not on the author's site) and is the one item still worth acquiring (medium); Poser 1986 (WCCFL 5) and Halle & Vergnaud 1987 are print/lending-only, low priority since they rest on the same Austin data. (Crowhurst and Pensalfini PDFs + txt; Trefry 1984 was already held by the project). all look-ups were by direct download (ROA index, Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, archive.org metadata, Cambridge Core, billposer.org).

new_statements.quote: To summarise, stress in Diyari is assigned (i) initially in morphemes of at least two syllables, but never to monosyllables, and (ii) to the third syllable of a quadrisyllabic, but never a trisyllabic morpheme.

new_statements.locator: §3 'Diyari', p. 9 of the ROA PDF (summary); data on pp. 1-2, exx. (1a) and (3), cited to Austin 1981:31 and Poser 1989:119
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial (primary) stress on the root, a secondary stress on the third syllable of four-syllable morphemes, secondary stress on the first syllable of each disyllabic suffix, no stress on monosyllabic suffixes or word-finally. This is a restatement of Austin 1981 and Poser 1989, not first-hand field data, so it confirms the catalog's fixed-dominant coding and its secondary-stress rule without adding a new primary witness. Pensalfini 2000 (§2.2, p. 2) says the same in its own words (roots initial, disyllabic suffixes stressed on their first syllable, monosyllabic suffixes never stressed), also from Austin 1981.

sources.quote: "Stress in Diyari is not phonologically contrastive and is entirely predictable from the shapes of roots and suffix morphemes. Primary stress falls on the first vowel of a root and secondary stress is assigned to the third vowel of a four syllable root (no roots are longer than four syllables). Disyllabic suffix morphemes are assigned (secondary) stress on their first syllable; this can result in sequences of unstressed syllables. Note that word-final syllables are never stress[ed] in Diyari." (

sources.citation: Crowhurst, Megan J. (1994). Prosodic alignment and misalignment in Diyari, Dyirbal, and Gooniyandi: an optimizing approach. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-19, 10 pp.
sources.quote: p. 1: "Diyari (Austin 1981, Poser 1989), Dyirbal (Dixon 1972), and Gooniyandi (McGregor 1990), languages of Australia, are metrically similar in assigning stress initially in all morphemes containing at least two syllables. In Diyari and Gooniyandi, the third syllable of a quadrisyllabic morpheme is also stressed. ... (1)a. Diyari (Austin 1981:31) pínadu 'old man' kán.a-wàr.a 'man-pl.' Nándawàlka 'to close' pínadu-wàr.a 'old man-pl.'" p. 9: "To summarise, stress in Diyari is assigned (i) initially in morphemes of at least two syllables, but never to monosyllables, and (ii) to the third syllable of a quadrisyllabic, but never a trisyllabic morpheme."
sources.locator: §1 p. 1 (ex. 1a, 'Austin 1981:31'), p. 2 (ex. 3, forms cited to Austin 1981 pages and Poser 1989:119), §3 summary p. 9
sources.note: Secondary OT analysis built on Austin 1981 and Poser 1989 (forms cited to page). Initial stress in every morpheme of two or more syllables; third syllable of a four-syllable morpheme also stressed; monosyllabic suffixes never stressed, even in sequence (e.g. (púdi)-ya-ni-wu); feet are quantity-insensitive disyllabic trochees that never straddle a morpheme boundary. Ranking FtBin, Tauto-F >> MFL >> Parse-σ.

sources.citation: Pensalfini, Rob (2000). Suffix coherence and stress in Australian languages. Proceedings of the 1999 Conference of the Australian Linguistic Society, 15 pp.
sources.quote: §2, p. 1-2: "The five languages can be characterised in the same way with respect to stress on monomorphemic words: stress falls on the first syllable and on every second syllable thereafter, but never on the final syllable (the distinction between primary and secondary stress is ignored). None of these languages allow adjacent stressed syllables." §2.2, p. 2: "Diyari, illustrated in (2), never allows a foot to contain nuclei from different morphemes at all. The result is that disyllabic suffixes will be stressed on their first syllable, while monosyllabic suffixes will never receive stress. (2) a. (kárna)-(wàra) man-PL b. (márda)-la-nhi hill-CHAR-LOC c. (kána)-nhi-(màtha) man-LOC-IDENT d. (pína)du-(wàra) old_man-PL e. (púlyu)da-nhi mud-LOC"
sources.locator: §2 p. 1-2 (general statement for the five languages) and §2.2 'Diyari' p. 2, ex. (2); data 'from Austin 1981:31 except where otherwise noted'
sources.note: Secondary source (data from Austin 1981; some stresses 'calculated' from Austin's description). Initial stress on roots, alternating within a morpheme, never final; feet never straddle a morpheme boundary; disyllabic suffixes stressed on their first syllable, monosyllabic suffixes never stressed. Comparative OT paper (Pintupi, Diyari, Dyirbal, Warlpiri, Jingulu); primary/secondary distinction deliberately ignored.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 1999 Annual meeting of the Australian Linguistics Society
